passage:
Subject: Why I'm learning a bit of everything

Dear Charu,

You asked why I signed up for a presenting course and a database class when I'm supposed to be a developer. Let me explain.

I don't know yet what I'll love. I liked building screens, but I also liked working out why numbers looked odd. My thinking is: if I can explain things clearly, work with data, and know how to put a project online, I can move in several directions and choose later when I can see what I'm drawn to.

It may feel scattered. I might be slower to specialise. But at twenty-four, I'd rather keep the doors open than close one by guessing.

What do you think?

Raghav

passage: Sabina, you asked why I'm doing a cloud basics course when I don't even know if I'll stay in tech. That's exactly why. I'm Neelam, I'm twenty-four, and honestly I don't know if in five years I'll want to build software, manage people or move into something like climate data. So I asked myself, what's useful in all three? Writing clearly. Talking to people who aren't engineers. Handling data without panic. Knowing how cloud systems work at a basic level. That's what I'm building this year: I present at the team demo every month, I do a data course on weekends, and now this cloud one. When I know what I love, I'll specialise. Until then, I'm packing a bag that fits any trip.

passage: I'm Himani, and I trained Yash when he joined our support team. He was never sure what he wanted. 'Maybe product, maybe data, maybe I'll go back and study,' he said in his first week. What I noticed was what he did with that uncertainty. He volunteered to write our help articles, so he got good at explaining. He asked the data team if he could clean the ticket reports on Fridays. He took a free cloud basics course and passed it on his second try. When our company launched a new product last year, they needed someone who could talk to customers, read the numbers and understand the servers a little. Yash was the only one on the list who could do all three. He still says he isn't sure. He just says it more calmly.

qa.a: It suggests he now feels secure rather than anxious about uncertainty, because his broad skills keep options open.

qa.a: He could notice which part of the role he enjoys most, customers, numbers or servers, and let that guide where he specialises.

qa.q: How does Himani see Yash's path?
qa.a: Himani, who trained Yash, sees someone who turned uncertainty into useful, transferable skills.

grounding: It shows a colleague watching someone unsure of the future build transferable skills in communication, data and cloud basics, leaving specialisation for later.
